To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the optimal per-node capacity scaling of the network is \Theta (\sqrt {M/m}) for a broad class (including Zipf distributions with any exponent 1) of popularity distributions, 2) the optimal per node caching strategy is to cache uniformly at random over the library, and 3) the throughput of the network scales with the network size $n$, i.e., the throughput per node is \Theta(1).

(i) for heavy tailed file popularity distributions, multihop device to device caching networks can significantly improve throughput scalability with the number of devices, and (ii) for Zipf popularity distributions with exponent larger than a threshold, the optimal throughput scalability can be achieved by ignoring less popular files in the cache.

(i) for heavy tailed file popularity distributions, the per node capacity scales as $\Theta \sqrt {m/M}$ for multihop caching networks, and (ii) for Zipf distributions with sufficiently large exponents, the per node throughput can be further improved by reducing the library size to the subset of most popular $K$ files, where $K$ can be selected to achieve a desired tradeoff between per node capacity and library size.

the design and analysis of wireless multihop device-to-device networks for caching, where nodes can serve as servers and/or clients in the network.
